<header class="tour-header">
  <span class="tour-eyebrow">Arizona Food Forest Tour</span>

  <h1>Tiny Phoenix Backyard Food Forest: Kim’s 24 Fruit Trees</h1>

  <div class="tour-category-row">
    <span class="tour-category">Phoenix</span>
    <span class="tour-category">Small-Space Growing</span>
    <span class="tour-category">Tropical Fruit</span>
    <span class="tour-category">Edible Landscaping</span>
  </div>

  <p class="tour-description">
    Step inside Kim’s compact Phoenix garden, where 24 fruit trees,
    tropical plants, edible groundcovers, flowering ornamentals, and
    carefully managed shade create an incredible amount of abundance in
    a very limited amount of growing space.
  </p>

  <div class="tour-meta">
    <div>
      <span class="meta-label">Host</span>
      <span class="meta-value">Kim</span>
    </div>
    <div>
      <span class="meta-label">Published</span>
      <span class="meta-value">August 28, 2026</span>
    </div>
  </div>
</header>

<p class="tour-lead">
Kim’s garden is a reminder that abundance does not require acres of land.
On a small northwest Phoenix property, she has built a diverse edible
landscape by fitting fruit trees, tropical plants, flowering species, and
useful shade plants into nearly every available pocket of space.
</p>

<section class="quick-facts" aria-label="Tour snapshot">
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Garden</span><span class="fact-value">Private Phoenix Food Forest</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Host</span><span class="fact-value">Kim</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Location</span><span class="fact-value">Northwest Phoenix, Arizona</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Fruit Trees</span><span class="fact-value">24</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Plantable Space</span><span class="fact-value">About 110 ft × 11 ft</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Growing Style</span><span class="fact-value">Compact & High-Diversity</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Primary Challenge</span><span class="fact-value">Heat, Wind & Limited Space</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Tour Length</span><span class="fact-value">About 35 Minutes</span></div>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>How Much Can You Grow in a Tiny Phoenix Yard?</h2>
<p>
Kim’s property is a corner lot with very little plantable ground and an
oversized swimming pool occupying much of the backyard. Instead of treating
those limitations as reasons not to grow food, she has spent years learning
how to use small planting strips, containers, narrow side yards, and carefully
chosen pockets around the house.
</p>
<p>
By the end of the tour, Kim counts 24 fruit trees on the property. She estimates
that she has only about 110 feet by 11 feet of practical planting space. The
result is not a traditional orchard with large trees spaced far apart. It is a
dense collection of compact trees, tropical plants, vines, groundcovers,
flowers, and useful ornamentals fitted together around the realities of the
property.
</p>
<div class="tour-highlight">
<strong>The central lesson of Kim’s garden</strong>
<p>
You do not need acres of land to create an abundant edible landscape.
Kim’s yard shows what can happen when limited space is treated as a design
challenge rather than a reason not to plant.
</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>A Garden Designed Around the Phoenix Sun</h2>
<p>
One of the clearest patterns in Kim’s garden is how intentionally she thinks
about exposure. Her corner property has very little protection from western
sun and wind, so different areas of the yard are used for different types of
plants.
</p>
<p>
The east side of the house is especially important for tropicals. During the
hottest part of summer, that side begins receiving automatic afternoon shade.
Kim explains that this is where she concentrates many of the plants that need
relief from the most intense June, July, and August sun.
</p>
<p>
Elsewhere, temporary plants and vines become part of the shade system. Castor
beans can grow quickly enough to create seasonal protection, while vines are
allowed to cover the pergola during summer and then removed in winter so the
mangoes below can receive more sun.
</p>
<p>
Bamboo also plays a role. On the west side of the pergola, it helps block late
afternoon summer sun that was reaching the mango trees after the overhead
shade had already been established.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Keeping Fruit Trees Small on Purpose</h2>
<p>
Kim repeatedly points out that many of her trees are intentionally kept
compact. Part of that decision comes from the size of the property, but it is
also about making the garden easier to manage.
</p>
<p>
Her Pakistan mulberry has grown aggressively enough that she regularly has to
cut back several feet of growth. She ultimately decides that the tree may need
to leave the yard because of how quickly it occupies space. Other trees are
pruned to stay within reach instead of becoming full-size specimens.
</p>
<p>
That same principle shows up throughout the property. A limequat that could
become much larger is kept small. White sapote, mango, starfruit, Barbados
cherry, citrus, and ornamentals are all managed within the scale of the yard.
Kim is designing for a garden she can continue enjoying rather than maximizing
the ultimate height of every tree.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Mangoes in a Small-Space Phoenix Food Forest</h2>
<p>
Mangoes appear throughout Kim’s garden, and several have unusual stories.
Some began as nursery discards that still had enough life left in them to be
rescued and planted. One front-yard mango has remained relatively compact
while producing heavily.
</p>
<p>
On the east side, a Carrie mango is recovering after a period when the garden
received less care. Another older mango planted in 2017 had once grown above
the roofline before suffering badly and beginning a new recovery cycle.
</p>
<p>
Near the pond, Kim originally imagined creating a larger mango-growing zone.
As her interest in the pond increased, the pond expanded and the mango space
became smaller. Three mango trees remain in that area, surrounded by a system
that changes with the seasons.
</p>
<p>
Summer vines create shade overhead, while winter removal allows more sunlight
into the area. Several of the mangoes also receive water drawn directly from
the pond.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Fruit Trees Packed Into the Landscape</h2>
<p>
The variety in Kim’s compact garden is what makes the tour especially
surprising. Mangoes share the property with subtropical fruit, citrus,
traditional Arizona fruit trees, and a large collection of tropical and
flowering plants.
</p>
<div class="plant-grid">
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Mango</strong><span>Several trees, including Carrie mango and rescued nursery trees.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Longan</strong><span>A young tree that has surprised Kim with its tolerance of the sunny site.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Starfruit</strong><span>A productive tree that fruits repeatedly and has performed well in the yard.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Limequat</strong><span>One of Kim’s favorite fruits, eaten fresh for its aromatic skin and tart interior.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>White Guava</strong><span>A compact tree that produced a substantial winter crop before cycling into new growth.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>White Sapote</strong><span>A Redlands white sapote kept within the scale of the small yard.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Florida Prince Peach</strong><span>A low-chill peach that produced hundreds of fruit in a stronger season.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Barbados Cherry</strong><span>A fast-growing tree planted in 2017 and heavily pruned to stay manageable.</span></div>
  <div class="plant-card"><strong>Papaya</strong><span>Seed-grown papaya used as a temporary layer while longer-lived trees establish nearby.</span></div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Tropical Plants, Flowers, and Useful Fillers</h2>
<p>
Kim’s yard is not made up of fruit trees alone. Plumerias, hibiscus, cannas,
sweet almond bush, tropical milkweed, vines, bamboo, sweet potato, monstera,
elephant food, and other plants occupy the spaces between trees.
</p>
<p>
Some are there primarily because they are beautiful. Others have practical
jobs. Sweet potato covers and cools exposed soil. Castor bean can become quick
summer shade. Bamboo blocks unwanted views and intense afternoon sun. Tropical
milkweed supports monarch butterflies. Flowering plants add color and habitat
throughout the food forest.
</p>
<p>
The result feels less like a conventional orchard and more like a compact,
layered edible landscape where fruit production, shade, privacy, pollinators,
and aesthetics all overlap.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>The Recovery Yard</h2>
<p>
An important part of Kim’s story is that the garden has not moved forward in a
perfect straight line. She explains that during a difficult period of her life,
many plants received far less care than they normally would have.
</p>
<p>
Some trees were lost. Others were badly stressed. Several of the trees shown
during the tour are in the process of rebuilding growth rather than displaying
their full potential.
</p>
<p>
Kim describes the property as a “recovery yard.” That makes the garden more
interesting, not less. Visitors are seeing a real landscape where plants have
been neglected, moved, cut back, replanted, reconsidered, and given another
chance.
</p>
<p>
Her older mango is a good example. After declining badly, Kim uncovered a
buried root flare, increased attention, added shade, and watched the tree begin
pushing strong recovery growth again.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>A Pond That Changed the Garden</h2>
<p>
What began as a small pond eventually became one of Kim’s favorite parts of
the backyard. As the pond expanded, it changed the original planting plan and
reduced the number of mangoes that could remain in the area.
</p>
<p>
The pond also became part of how nearby mango trees are managed. Kim lowers
the water level, mixes the nutrient-rich material from the fish system, and
uses a sump pump to move pond water into the surrounding mango zone.
</p>
<p>
More importantly, the pond shows how gardens evolve around the people who live
in them. The most “efficient” use of the space might have been to keep every
mango tree. Kim discovered that she enjoyed the pond more, so the food forest
changed with her.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Plants With Jobs</h2>
<p>
Kim often chooses plants based on what she needs a particular location to do.
A Barbados cherry helps block early sunlight from reaching the bedroom. Another
guava is being grown to eventually provide shade at a different time of day.
Bamboo screens a distracting view. Seasonal vines protect mangoes from summer
sun.
</p>
<p>
That way of thinking is especially useful in a small landscape because every
square foot matters. A plant can produce fruit while also creating privacy,
cooling the house, shading another plant, covering the soil, or improving the
way a space feels.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Plants Featured in Kim’s Phoenix Garden</h2>
<p>
The tour moves through an unusually diverse plant collection. The list below
collects many of the fruiting, edible, flowering, and tropical plants Kim
mentions during the visit.
</p>

<details class="plant-details">
<summary>View the expanded plant list</summary>
<div class="plant-details-content">
<ul>
  <li>Green Indian jujube</li>
  <li>Royal poinciana</li>
  <li>Plumeria</li>
  <li>Mango</li>
  <li>Sumo orange</li>
  <li>Monstera</li>
  <li>Natal plum</li>
  <li>Cassia fistula / golden shower tree</li>
  <li>Morning glory bush</li>
  <li>Surinam cherry</li>
  <li>Sweet almond bush</li>
  <li>Tropical milkweed</li>
  <li>June plum</li>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>The Green Yard Takeaway</h2>
<div class="takeaway">
<p>
Kim’s Phoenix garden demonstrates that abundance is not simply a function of
property size. Her landscape works because she is willing to keep trees small,
use different exposures intentionally, let plants perform multiple jobs, and
continually reconsider how the limited space should be used.
</p>
<p>
The garden is also still changing. Some trees are recovering, new fruit trees
are waiting to be planted, the pond may grow again, and Kim is already thinking
about how different areas will look in another year or two. That ongoing
evolution is part of what makes the property worth revisiting.
</p>
</div>
</section>
